1.title: Manage the Lifecycle of Data
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Manage the Lifecycle of Data. This module covers the task statement: manage the lifecycle of data. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Move data between Amazon S three and Amazon Redshift with copy and unload. Use S three Lifecycle policies to change storage tiers and expire data. Manage S three versioning and DynamoDB T T L (time to live). Delete data to meet business and legal requirements. Protect data with the right resiliency and availability. --.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Ages Its Data
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Ages Its Data. Last month's orders are queried daily; older months almost never. Raw files may be deleted after two years, but invoices must be kept seven years. A customer asks Kestrel to erase their personal data. Your job: keep hot data fast, cold data cheap, and deletions provable.

1.title: Loading and Unloading Between S3 and Redshift
1.text: Loading and Unloading Between S three and Redshift. The figure shows this: copy loads from Amazon S three into Amazon Redshift in parallel; unload writes query results from Redshift back to Amazon S three, for example as partitioned Parquet files.

1.title: Loading and Unloading Between S3 and Redshift, continued
1.text: Loading and Unloading Between S three and Redshift, continued. copy. Direction: S three to Redshift (also from DynamoDB, E M R (Elastic MapReduce) and remote hosts). Remember: Parallel load across slices; I A M (Identity and Access Management) role to read S three; formats C S V, Jason, Avro, Parquet, O R C (Optimized Row Columnar); compression options (gzip, Zstandard, bzip two, L Z O P); manifest file lists exact files; M A X E R R O R; splittable and similar-size files load fastest (Module one). unload. Direction: Redshift to S three. Remember: Writes result files in parallel (several files); can write Parquet, partition by columns, encrypt with K M S (Key Management Service), overwrite, and write a manifest; use it to archive old data or hand data to the lake.

1.title: Loading and Unloading Between S3 and Redshift, continued
1.text: Loading and Unloading Between S three and Redshift, continued. Auto-copy or copy job. Direction: S three to Redshift, automatically. Remember: Loads new files from an S three prefix as they arrive. Typical lifecycle: hot data in Redshift tables to unload older partitions to S three as Parquet to delete them from Redshift to still queryable through Redshift Spectrum (Module six). Loading best practices: copy, not row inserts; one copy per table over a prefix; compress; verify loaded row counts and errors (S T L load errors). Exam tip: "Move old rows out of Redshift to cheap storage and still query them" to unload to S three as Parquet, then query with Redshift Spectrum. "Load many files fast" to copy (not insert).

1.title: S3 Lifecycle Policies: Tiering and Expiring
1.text: S three Lifecycle Policies: Tiering and Expiring. The figure shows this: An S three Lifecycle rule moves objects down the storage classes as they age and finally expires them; noncurrent versions and incomplete uploads can have their own shorter rules.

1.title: Lifecycle actions
1.text: Lifecycle actions. Transition. Moves objects to a cheaper storage class after N days. Expiration. Deletes current objects after N days (in a versioned bucket it adds a delete marker). Noncurrent version transition or expiration. Moves or permanently deletes older versions after N days. Abort incomplete multipart uploads. Cleans up unfinished uploads. Filters. By prefix, tags, object size (ObjectSizeGreaterThan or LessThan).

1.title: Rules to remember
1.text: Rules to remember. Waterfall model: objects move down the classes: Standard to Standard-I A (Infrequent Access) to Glacier Instant Retrieval to Glacier Flexible Retrieval to Glacier Deep Archive (also One Zone-I A and Intelligent-Tiering); Deep Archive is one way (restore, then copy, to move back). Objects smaller than one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes do not transition by default (the request cost can exceed the saving); change it with an object size filter. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Rules to remember, continued
1.text: Rules to remember, continued. Minimum storage durations are charged on early exit: Standard-I A thirty days, Glacier Instant and Flexible ninety, Deep Archive one hundred eighty; you cannot move an object on before its minimum period has passed in one rule. Glacier overhead: each archived object adds about forty kilobytes of metadata (eight kilobytes at Standard rates, thirty-two kilobytes at the archive rate): combine many small objects before archiving. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Rules to remember, continued
1.text: Rules to remember, continued. Archived objects are not instantly available: restore first (Flexible Retrieval: expedited one to five minutes, standard three to five hours, bulk five to twelve hours; Deep Archive: standard twelve hours, bulk forty-eight hours). Lifecycle runs asynchronously (a delay between the rule date and the physical change; billing follows the rule date for archive classes). Intelligent-Tiering moves objects automatically when the access pattern is unknown (objects under one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes are not tiered). Exam tip: "Keep data ninety days for fast access, then archive for years at the lowest cost, then delete" to an S three Lifecycle rule: transition to Glacier classes, then expire. "Unknown or changing access pattern" to S three Intelligent-Tiering. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: S3 versioning
1.text: S three versioning. Versioning keeps every version of an object; an overwrite creates a new version, a delete adds a delete marker (the older versions remain and cost storage). Protects against accidental delete and overwrite; you can restore an earlier version. States: unversioned, enabled, suspended (a bucket cannot go back to unversioned). To really delete, delete specific versions or use lifecycle rules for noncurrent versions (expire after N days, keep the last N versions). Add M F A (multi-factor authentication) delete and S three Object Lock (W O R M, retention and legal hold) for tamper-proof retention. Versioning plus replication supports recovery and disaster protection.

1.title: DynamoDB TTL (time to live)
1.text: DynamoDB T T L (time to live). T T L deletes expired items automatically: enable it on a table and name a T T L attribute holding an expiry time as a Number in Unix epoch seconds. Expired items are removed in the background, typically within a few days after expiry, without using write capacity; until then they can still be read, so filter them out of queries. Deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions, so a stream consumer can archive expired items to S three; with global tables the delete is replicated. Use T T L for sessions, temporary records and old telemetry. Exam tip: "Automatically remove DynamoDB items after thirty days at no throughput cost" to T T L with an epoch-seconds attribute. "Recover an accidentally overwritten S three object" to versioning.

2.title: Deleting Data to Meet Business and Legal Needs
2.text: Deleting Data to Meet Business and Legal Needs. Why delete: retention schedules, privacy laws (for example a right to erasure), contracts, and cost; keep data only as long as it is needed, and keep it as long as the law requires. Retention versus deletion: legal hold and W O R M (write once, read many) (S three Object Lock) stop deletion; a retention policy says when deletion must happen. Automate: S three Lifecycle expiration, DynamoDB T T L, scheduled deletes in Redshift and R D S (Relational Database Service), backup retention settings. Deleting from files in a lake is hard: immutable files (Parquet) must be rewritten; Apache Iceberg row-level deletes (and S three Tables) make targeted erasure practical.

2.title: Deleting Data to Meet Business and Legal Needs, continued
2.text: Deleting Data to Meet Business and Legal Needs, continued. Copies matter: erase from every copy: replicas, backups and snapshots, derived tables, caches, logs; a delete marker or a soft delete is not erasure. Prove it: log the deletion (CloudTrail, job logs) and keep an audit record without the personal data. Encryption helps: deleting a K M S key makes data encrypted under it unreadable (crypto-shredding), but key deletion has a waiting period and affects everything under that key. Exam tip: "Remove one customer's data from a Parquet lake on request" to Iceberg row-level delete (or rewrite the affected files), and remove it from backups and copies, not a lifecycle rule.

2.title: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data
2.text: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data. Amazon S three. Protection: Designed for eleven nines durability, data across multiple A Zs (Availability Zone); versioning; replication (same-Region or cross-Region); Object Lock. Remember: Replication needs versioning; S three Glacier classes keep the same durability. Amazon DynamoDB. Protection: Multi-A Z by default; point-in-time recovery (P I T R) up to thirty-five days; on-demand backups; global tables (multi-Region, active-active). Remember: P I T R (point-in-time recovery) restores to a new table. Amazon R D S or Aurora. Protection: Multi-A Z (standby for failover); automated backups (zero to thirty-five days) with point-in-time restore; manual snapshots; read replicas; Aurora storage is replicated six ways across three A Zs. Remember: Restores create a new instance.

2.title: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data, continued
2.text: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data, continued. Amazon Redshift. Protection: Automated and manual snapshots, cross-Region snapshot copy, Multi-A Z for R A three clusters, backups to S three. Remember: Choose retention to match the R P O (recovery point objective). Amazon E B S (Elastic Block Store) or E F S (Elastic File System). Protection: E B S snapshots; E F S is multi-A Z with backups and lifecycle to I A. A W S Backup. Protection: Central backup service: backup plans (schedule and retention), vaults, cross-Region and cross-account copies, Vault Lock (W O R M) across S three, DynamoDB, R D S, Aurora, E F S, E B S, Redshift and more. Remember: One policy for many services. R P O (recovery point objective): how much data you can lose (time between backups); R T O (recovery time objective) (recovery time objective): how long recovery may take.

2.title: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data, continued
2.text: Resiliency and Availability of Stored Data, continued. Choose the strategy by R P O and R T O: backups (cheapest, slowest), cross-Region replication and global tables (lowest R P O and R T O). Test restores: an untested backup is not a recovery plan. Availability versus durability: availability equals can you reach it now (Multi-A Z, replicas); durability equals will the data survive (replication, backups). Exam tip: "Centrally manage backup schedules and retention across S three, R D S, DynamoDB and E F S, with cross-Region copies" to A W S Backup. "Restore a DynamoDB table to any second in the last thirty-five days" to point-in-time recovery.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. copy or unload: copy S three to Redshift in parallel (manifest, compression, formats); unload Redshift to S three (Parquet, partitions, K M S). S three Lifecycle: Transition (waterfall, one-way to Deep Archive), expiration, noncurrent versions, abort multipart. Retrieval: Flexible: one to five min or three to five h or five to twelve h; Deep Archive: twelve h or forty-eight h. Versioning: Every version kept; delete equals delete marker; cannot revert to unversioned; lifecycle for noncurrent versions. T T L: Epoch-seconds Number; deleted within a few days, no write capacity; shows in Streams. Deleting: Retention schedules; all copies and backups; Iceberg row-level delete; delete marker ≠ erasure; log the proof. Resilience: S three eleven nines, versioning, replication; DynamoDB P I T R thirty-five days, global tables.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Kestrel Freight keeps the last twelve months of order data in Amazon Redshift. Older data is rarely queried but must remain queryable. What is the most cost-effective approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. unload writes older data to cheap S three in a columnar format, and Spectrum lets Redshift users still query it without loading it.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Objects in an S three bucket must stay in Standard for thirty days, move to an archive class for seven years, and then be deleted automatically. What should be configured? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Lifecycle rules transition objects between storage classes and expire them by age without code.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A DynamoDB table holds user sessions that should disappear after twenty-four hours at no extra throughput cost. What should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. T T L deletes expired items in the background without consuming write capacity; the attribute must be a Number in epoch seconds.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Select two. A customer requests erasure of their personal data. The data is in Parquet files in S three, in Redshift and in backups. Which two actions are part of a correct approach? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Erasure must reach all copies, and immutable files need row-level deletes or rewrites. A delete marker only hides the object, archiving keeps the data, and disabling logging removes the proof.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A company wants one policy to back up S three, R D S, DynamoDB and E F S, with copies in another Region and W O R M protection. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A W S Backup centralizes backup plans across services and supports cross-Region copy and Vault Lock.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: D. Question two: C. Question three: B. Question four: C and E. Question five: C. In the next module, we continue the course.
